prompt_free_text:
This paper addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between standard motion forecasting benchmarks and real deployment: in practice, forecasting is performed continuously over time, whereas most benchmark methods process each scene independently. The paper proposes RealMotion, which augments a fairly simple encoder-decoder backbone with two temporal mechanisms operating across successive sub-scenes: a scene context stream that propagates scene-level context, and an agent trajectory stream that relays past predictions through a trajectory memory bank. The authors also introduce a data reorganization procedure that converts standard benchmark scenes into short continuous sequences by splitting trajectories at multiple historical timestamps. Empirically, the method reports strong results on Argoverse 2 and competitive results on Argoverse 1, along with ablations and an efficiency discussion.

I think the paper’s central motivation is compelling. The observation that repeated online forecasting should exploit temporal continuity across successive inference calls is intuitively correct and practically relevant. This is a real gap in much of the literature, which often optimizes one-shot forecasting under benchmark-specific assumptions. The paper also has a nice systems flavor: it does not only propose a temporal model, but also tries to reconcile existing datasets with the continuous-driving setting through data restructuring. That combination of problem reframing plus method design is a strength.

The empirical results are also promising. On Argoverse 2 single-agent forecasting, the reported gains over QCNet on minFDE1 and minADE1 are substantial, and the method remains competitive on the other leaderboard metrics. The multi-agent results are also strong despite the method not being explicitly designed around a joint multi-agent decoder. The ablations suggest that both the reorganized continuous data and the two temporal streams contribute. The efficiency section is useful as well, especially because the paper’s practical motivation would be weakened if the method were prohibitively expensive.

That said, I have several concerns about the paper’s technical clarity, experimental fairness, and the strength of the causal claims being made.

The biggest issue is that the paper mixes together three distinct contributions—data reorganization, scene-context recurrence, and trajectory-memory refinement—and it is not always clear which component is responsible for which gains, or whether the comparisons to prior work are apples-to-apples. In particular, the main leaderboard comparison contrasts RealMotion against methods trained and evaluated in the standard benchmark setting, while RealMotion is trained on a transformed dataset that effectively creates multiple temporally related sub-scenes from each original sample. Although the authors argue this better matches deployment, it also changes the supervision structure and potentially the amount and nature of training signal. The ablation with “continuous data only” helps, but it does not fully resolve the fairness question. A stronger evaluation would compare against strong baselines retrained under the same reorganized-data regime, not only the authors’ own stripped-down variant. The appendix result “QCNet w/ RealMotion data” is a step in this direction, but it is too limited: only one baseline is tested, only the data reorganization is transferred, and the implementation details are sparse. This leaves open whether much of the gain comes simply from training on more correlated sub-scenes rather than from the proposed temporal architecture.

Relatedly, the paper’s claim of “state of the art” should be interpreted carefully. The strongest gains are on minFDE1/minADE1, while QCNet remains slightly better on minFDE6. Since the method is explicitly designed to refine predictions over time, it would be useful to understand whether it mainly sharpens the top mode rather than improving calibrated multimodality. In fact, several ablation comments already hint that the temporal streams help single-mode metrics more than six-mode metrics. This is interesting, but it also suggests a narrower benefit than the headline might imply. A deeper analysis of mode diversity, calibration, and whether the memory bank collapses uncertainty would strengthen the paper.

A second major concern is the exact formulation of the continuous setting and whether it risks information leakage or unrealistic supervision. The data reorganization procedure is described as retrospectively splitting each benchmark scene into multiple sub-scenes by selecting split points along the historical trajectory and extending into the future. However, the description is not sufficiently precise to rule out subtle leakage or train/test mismatch. For example, when constructing sub-scenes at later split points, what map and neighboring-agent context is available? Is it strictly limited to what would be observable at that timestamp, or does the retrospective construction use future-presence information to decide which agents or map elements to include? The text says surrounding agents within a certain range and local map are aggregated “for interested agents at each split point,” which sounds reasonable, but the implementation details matter a lot here. Similarly, because all segments come from the same original scene, gradients are computed for all segments jointly. This may create a training regime that is richer than true online inference, where only past states are available and errors accumulate causally. The paper should be much more explicit about what is and is not available at each step, ideally with pseudocode and a leakage audit.

The online/offline distinction in the efficiency section also needs clarification. The paper reports 20 ms online latency and 62 ms offline latency for RealMotion, with the explanation that offline evaluation effectively incurs three iterations while online use can amortize computation because each intermediate prediction is meaningful. This is plausible, but the comparison is not fully convincing as presented. First, the paper should specify exactly what is cached between steps, what fraction of the encoder is recomputed, and whether the reported online latency includes memory-bank updates and coordinate transforms. Second, the comparison to HPTR’s online latency is not necessarily fair unless both methods are measured under the same streaming protocol and caching assumptions. Since efficiency is one of the paper’s selling points, this section should be more rigorous.

On the modeling side, the proposed architecture is sensible but somewhat incremental. The scene context stream is essentially temporal cross-attention between current and previous scene features after alignment, and the trajectory stream is a memory-based refinement module over prior predicted trajectories. Both are reasonable designs, but the novelty is moderate. The scene context stream especially resembles a straightforward recurrent extension of scene encoders with cross-attention and pose alignment. The trajectory stream is more distinctive, but even there the core idea—retrieve similar historical predictions and refine current outputs—is conceptually close to memory-based temporal smoothing. This does not invalidate the contribution, but it means the paper’s impact depends heavily on careful validation that these simple mechanisms truly solve a meaningful practical problem rather than just exploiting benchmark restructuring.

I also found the method description occasionally underspecified or confusing. Equation (1) uses MLN with positional encoding of relative pose and time, but it is not clear whether MLN alone is sufficient to “project” features between coordinate systems, or whether this is better interpreted as conditioning normalization on relative motion rather than geometric transformation. Equation (2) overwrites the current features with pure cross-attention outputs; are residual connections and feed-forward layers used, as in standard Transformer blocks? Equation (3) for trajectory alignment is difficult to parse, especially the choice of origin y_i^{ori} = y_i[Δt · q]. More explanation is needed for how trajectories from different historical times are aligned to the current frame, especially when Δt varies and when the stored prediction horizon only partially overlaps the current forecast horizon. Equation (4) also introduces symbols F_mo, Y_mo, F_b, Y_b without enough context on tensor shapes, number of retrieved bank entries, or whether retrieval is all-to-all or truncated. These details matter for reproducibility.

The training setup raises additional questions. The loss uses equal weights for regression, classification, and refinement, but there is no justification or sensitivity analysis. The model predicts a singular trajectory for auxiliary training of other agents, but this auxiliary objective is barely described and not reflected in the loss equation. It is also unclear how the memory bank is handled during training: are ground-truth previous predictions ever used (teacher forcing), or is the bank populated only with model predictions? If the latter, how is instability early in training controlled? If the former, there may be exposure bias issues at test time. This is especially important because the method’s core premise is sequential prediction over time.

The experimental section is generally solid, but several comparisons could be stronger. Argoverse 1 results are reported on validation rather than test, while Argoverse 2 uses leaderboard test results; this makes cross-dataset conclusions less clean. The paper cites a temporal benchmark based on tracking data as related work, but does not compare directly against streaming/temporal forecasting methods in a controlled setting. Since the paper’s main claim is about continuous forecasting, a direct comparison to prior streaming formulations would be very valuable. In addition, the qualitative examples are suggestive but limited. The paper would benefit from analyses on scenarios where temporal continuity should matter most: occlusions, partial observability, lane changes, interactions at intersections, and long-tail maneuvers. The motivating example in Figure 1 mentions perceiving a currently invisible pedestrian, but I did not see a quantitative evaluation specifically targeting such cases.

Another concern is generalization and benchmark dependence. The authors acknowledge that the method relies on sufficient historical frames and may not apply to datasets like Waymo with shorter history. This is an important limitation, and in my view it somewhat narrows the claimed generality of the framework. More broadly, because the method derives its temporal sequence by slicing a single benchmark scene, it is not obvious how well the learned recurrence would transfer to truly long-horizon streaming operation in a deployed stack, where perception noise, tracking identity switches, and map updates all matter. The paper would be stronger if it discussed these deployment assumptions more explicitly.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. The problem framing is valuable, the method is practical, and the empirical gains are nontrivial. My overall assessment is positive but not without reservations. The main reasons are that the paper identifies a meaningful blind spot in current forecasting practice and offers a lightweight temporal extension that appears effective. However, for a top-tier venue, I would want stronger evidence that the gains are not primarily due to the reorganized training setup, clearer guarantees about causal validity and absence of leakage, and more rigorous evaluation of the true online setting.

The most important improvements I would request are the following. First, add stronger baseline retraining under the same continuous-data protocol, ideally including at least two competitive methods beyond QCNet, so the contribution of the architecture can be isolated from the contribution of the data restructuring. Second, provide a precise algorithmic description of the data reorganization and online inference pipeline, including what information is available at each split point and how caching is implemented. Third, analyze whether the method improves multimodal uncertainty or mainly the top-1 mode, for example via diversity/calibration metrics or oracle-vs-ranked performance breakdowns. Fourth, include targeted evaluations on scenarios where temporal continuity should matter most, such as occlusions and interaction-heavy scenes. Fifth, clarify the training dynamics of the memory bank and whether teacher forcing is used.

In summary, this is an interesting and practically motivated paper with strong reported results and a sensible temporal design. Its main weakness is that the experimental protocol changes the problem setting in a way that complicates fair comparison and attribution of gains. If the authors can better disentangle the effects of data restructuring versus model design and clarify the causal online setup, the work would be significantly stronger.

My recommendation is a weak accept to borderline accept, assuming the venue values practical reframing and strong empirical performance. If the bar is very high on methodological novelty and airtight evaluation protocol, this could also land on the reject side.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes RealMotion, a motion forecasting framework for continuous driving that departs from the standard independent-scene formulation. The method reorganizes benchmark scenes into temporally ordered sub-scenes, then applies two recurrent temporal mechanisms: a scene context stream that propagates historical scene features via cross-attention after coordinate alignment, and an agent trajectory stream that stores prior predicted trajectories/features in a memory bank and refines current predictions using trajectory-conditioned attention. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2, including single-agent and multi-agent settings, report strong leaderboard performance and ablations suggesting gains from both the data reorganization and the two temporal streams, while maintaining relatively small model size and competitive online latency.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment: motion forecasting is repeatedly executed over temporally connected scenes rather than isolated snapshots.
The proposed decomposition into a scene context stream and an agent trajectory stream is intuitive and practically motivated, separating contextual accumulation from trajectory refinement.
Empirical results are strong on Argoverse 2 test leaderboard and competitive on Argoverse 1, with improvements over a broad set of baselines.
Ablation studies cover major components, including data reorganization, both streams, alignment modules, trajectory embedding, split points, gradient steps, and attention depth.
The method appears parameter-efficient relative to several strong baselines, and the paper discusses online vs offline latency explicitly.
The appendix includes some evidence that the reorganized continuous-scene data structure can also benefit another model (QCNet), supporting partial generality of the idea.
weaknesses: The central experimental claim is confounded by the custom data reorganization protocol: comparisons to prior methods are not apples-to-apples because RealMotion is trained/evaluated under a modified sequential setting while most baselines are reported from standard benchmark protocols.

The paper lacks a rigorous formalization of the continuous-driving task and evaluation protocol, especially how sub-scenes are generated, how overlap between segments affects supervision, and how final benchmark predictions are selected from sequential outputs.

There is potential train/test mismatch and possible information leakage risk in the reorganization procedure because each original scene is retrospectively split into overlapping sub-scenes with shared future horizons, but the paper does not carefully analyze whether this changes sample independence or effectively augments near-duplicate examples.

The trajectory memory bank uses past predictions rather than ground truth, but the paper does not analyze error accumulation, stability over long horizons, or robustness when earlier predictions are poor.

Methodological details are underspecified in several places: memory bank size n, retrieval policy, number of modes stored per agent, exact decoder design, how agents are associated across sub-scenes, and how missing/appearing agents are handled.

The claimed efficiency advantage is somewhat selective: offline latency is still substantially higher than the independent variant because three sequential passes are required, and comparisons are made to only a small set of baselines under unclear implementation parity.

The novelty is moderate, as the method combines known ingredients—feature alignment, cross-attention, memory banks, and trajectory refinement—into a sequential forecasting pipeline rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Some claims are overstated, e.g., 'state-of-the-art' and 'far outperformed most previous approaches,' despite mixed results across metrics where QCNet remains better on minFDE6 and tied/close on others.
methodological_flaws: Equation (1) does not actually define a geometrically correct projection from the previous local coordinate system to the current one; applying Motion-aware LayerNorm conditioned on relative pose is not equivalent to coordinate transformation. This weakens the scientific logic behind the claim that features are 'projected' or 'aligned' across scenes.

Equation (3) for trajectory alignment is mathematically unclear/incomplete. The transform uses only a rotation matrix and subtraction of an origin point y_i^{ori}=y_i[Δt·q], but does not clearly account for translation into the current ego frame, heading conventions, interpolation when Δt·q is non-integer, or truncation when the referenced index exceeds trajectory length.

The empirical comparison to standard leaderboard baselines is not fully valid as evidence for the proposed continuous-driving formulation, because those baselines generally do not exploit the reorganized sequential inputs. The stronger claim should be against reimplemented baselines under the same reorganized protocol, but only limited evidence is provided (mainly QCNet in appendix, and RealMotion-I as an internal baseline).

The data reorganization may create heavily overlapping training samples from the same original scene, which can inflate effective sample size and improve performance independently of the proposed temporal modeling. The paper does not control for this with a matched-data baseline beyond a single internal variant, nor quantify overlap effects rigorously.

The loss design uses equal weights for regression, classification, and refinement without justification or sensitivity analysis. Given that refinement is applied on top of initial predictions, equal weighting may bias optimization, yet no evidence is provided that this choice is principled or robust.

The paper claims lower real-world inference latency, but the reported offline evaluation requires multiple sequential passes and the online latency excludes details of state maintenance and agent association across time. Thus the practical efficiency claim is not fully substantiated.

There is no statistical analysis (e.g., variance across seeds, confidence intervals) for ablations or validation results, making it difficult to judge whether some reported gains—especially small differences in Tables 5 and 7—are significant.

The method relies on past predicted trajectories in memory, but there is no experiment comparing oracle memory (ground-truth past futures), no analysis of compounding errors over longer sequences, and no study of failure under distribution shift; this leaves the empirical validity of the trajectory stream only partially established.
